title: Humans Correct Their Judgements Through Debate, but Weaker AI Models Not
claim: A multi-stage protocol elicits prior beliefs, applies debate or consultancy, then measures belief updates after individual and group judgment.
layout: 6 numbered panels in two rows, left-to-right, arrows linking stages
description: A six-panel experimental pipeline in two rows. Row one has (1) General Pre-belief, (2) Specific Pre-belief and (3) Debate & Consultancy. Row two has (4) Specific Post-belief, (5) Collective Decision-Making and (6) a final Specific Post-belief. Green boxes with check marks mark correct statements, and red boxes with crosses mark incorrect ones. They sit beside icons for grounded judges (green person), erroneous judges (red person) and AI models (blue robot). Every panel uses the same example topic, 1970s US supersonic transport policy. Panel 3 shows 3 rounds of debate and a consultancy variant. Panel 4 splits into in-subtopic and cross-subtopic claims. Panel 5 shows chat bubbles of deliberation between humans and AI. Grey chevrons and a connector arrow show the flow. A legend at the bottom explains the icons.
caption: Full experimental pipeline and protocol variations, with human or LLM as supervisors.
abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations, varying (i) the type of judge (open source and proprietary LLMs, and human participants, N=507), (ii) the method for eliciting priors, and (iii) the specific claims debated, paired with different related claims subsequently evaluated for belief updating, to test whether corrections generalize across related subtopics. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges (from 41.3% to 57.6%, p = .028), whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, deliberation produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors (51.97% to 62.20%, p = 0.369), whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.
